text: About 2,600 years ago, Greek writers told of the Iberians of Spain’s eastern and southern coasts.
The whole Iberian Peninsula is named after them.
src: known from Greek and Roman writers from the 6th century BCE / the pre-Indo-European peoples of the eastern and southern coasts of the Iberian Peninsula / the peoples of the Spanish Levant
The Iberians gave their name to the whole peninsula

text: They lived in villages and in walled towns, led by chieftains and nobles.
They farmed, bred horses and dug silver, iron, tin and copper from the ground.
src: The Iberians lived in villages and in oppida, fortified settlements / Society was divided into kings or chieftains, nobles, priests, artisans and slaves
Farming, horses and mining sustained them / they worked the silver mines near Gadir and Carthago Nova, iron in the Ebro valley, and tin and copper

text: They worshipped many gods, such as an earth goddess linked with birds, flowers and wheat.
They burned their dead and laid the ashes in urns inside stone tombs.
src: Iberian religion was polytheistic / An important female deity of the earth and of renewal, linked with birds, flowers and wheat, appears in the Lady of Baza
The Iberians cremated their dead and placed the ashes in urns, which were laid in stone tombs

text: Iberian artists who knew Greek art well carved stone statues such as the Lady of Elche.
They painted pots with red patterns and wrote their language in scripts of their own.
src: The Lady of Baza and the Lady of Elche are thought to be the work of Iberians who knew Greek art well / The Iberians made sculpture in stone and bronze
Pots were mainly decorated with red geometric patterns / wrote in scripts of their own

text: Hannibal of Carthage conquered many Iberians, and most of them then fought for Carthage against Rome.
src: from 221 BCE Hannibal conquered the Iberians south of the Ebro, and Hannibal’s siege of Saguntum, an ally of Rome, began the Second Punic War. Iberians fought on both sides, most tribes for Carthage

text: Rome won that war, and over the years the Iberian language gave way to Latin.
The ruins of their towns, such as Ullastret, are still being uncovered and studied.
src: After the defeat of Carthage the Iberian territories were divided into two provinces / The Iberian language ... was gradually replaced by Latin
Their remains are still being uncovered and studied / the ruins of Ullastret are identified with Indika
